claims.text: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr has poor oxygen resistance that limits high-temperature performance.
The proposed intervention is to replace casting with gas-atomized powder metallurgy followed by hot-isostatic-pressing consolidation under high-purity inert gas or vacuum.
Inert- or vacuum-controlled powder processing will reduce oxygen pickup during alloy synthesis.
The intervention will produce a lower-oxygen microstructure with less dissolved oxygen.
The intervention will reduce internal oxide-inclusion levels.
Lower dissolved oxygen and fewer internal oxide inclusions will improve high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Powder metallurgy and HIP will retain a microstructure sufficiently similar to the cast state to preserve useful mechanical properties.
The processed alloy will show a significantly lower oxidation rate, mass gain, or oxide-scale formation than cast material during exposure in air at 1000 °C for 100 hours.
The processed alloy will retain 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
The processed alloy will retain a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
The expected benefits are bounded to exposures near 1000 °C for approximately 100 hours and to mechanical strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Longer exposures or substantially different loading rates may cause deviations from the predicted behavior.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis describes improved room-temperature oxygen resistance, whereas the specified test and the proposed benefit concern high-temperature oxidation resistance in air at 1000 °C.
